claim: Proteins localizing to the cisternal rim appear as rings in en face views and double-puncta in side views.
source: Assuming cisternae of a Golgi mini-stack are round membrane disks, we reasoned that these proteins must localize to the rim of their corresponding cisternae and their ring appearances must correspond to en face or oblique views (hereafter en face views) (Figure 1B). As expected for the orthogonal section of a ring (Figure 1B), side view images of Giantin, Golgin84 and GPP130 displayed a double-punctum, the connecting line of which is roughly orthogonal to the Golgi-axis (Figure 1C).
evidence: Logical inference from the geometry of cisternal structures combined with observed imaging patterns in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Giantin localizes to the cisternal rim of Golgi mini-stacks.
source: Airyscan super-resolution microscopy clearly revealed their staining patterns as rings (Figure 1A). Assuming cisternae of a Golgi mini-stack are round membrane disks, we reasoned that these proteins must localize to the rim of their corresponding cisternae and their ring appearances must correspond to en face or oblique views (hereafter en face views) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Ring patterns in super-resolution microscopy combined with geometric reasoning about cisternal structure.

claim: 68% of Golgi stacks in native NRK cells expressing GPP130-APEX2-GFP demonstrated predominant cisternal rim localization by EM.
source: Out of 57 Golgi stacks that we randomly imaged from 25 cells, 68% demonstrated a predominant cisternal rim localization in side or en face views (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), supporting the ring staining pattern observed.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of EM images shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rim localization of Giantin is corroborated by a previous immuno-EM study.
source: The rim localization of Giantin was also corroborated in a previous immuno-EM study, furthring supporting our data (Koreishi et al., 2013).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Koreishi et al., 2013.

claim: The mean diameter of Giantin-rings is 950 ± 10 nm (n = 336).
source: Among all Golgi markers, we observed that Giantin had the largest ring diameters—950 ± 10 nm (mean ± SEM, same for the rest; n = 336) (Figure 1H).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from microscopy images presented in Figure 1H.

claim: The epitope of the Giantin antibody used is at the N-terminus.
source: It is known that the epitope of our antibody is at the N-terminus while Giantin anchors onto the Golgi membrane via its extreme C-terminal transmembrane domain (Linstedt et al., 1995).
evidence: Reference to published work by Linstedt et al., 1995 and knowledge about the antibody used.

claim: Giantin anchors onto the Golgi membrane via its extreme C-terminal transmembrane domain.
source: It is known that the epitope of our antibody is at the N-terminus while Giantin anchors onto the Golgi membrane via its extreme C-terminal transmembrane domain (Linstedt et al., 1995).
evidence: Reference to published work by Linstedt et al., 1995.

claim: A fully extended Giantin molecule is predicted to reach 450 nm.
source: A fully extended Giantin molecule is predicted to reach 450 nm (Munro, 2011).
evidence: Reference to published work by Munro, 2011.

claim: The mean diameter of the Giantin C-terminus ring is approximately 50 nm smaller than that of the N-terminus ring.
source: Quantitative analysis revealed that the mean diameter of the C-terminus ring is ~50 nm smaller than that of the N-terminus one (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), far less than the value predicted for the fully extended molecule, which is 900 nm.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of microscopy data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The N- and C-termini of Giantin colocalize at the cisternal rim.
source: First, we raised an antibody against its C-terminal cytosolic region and ring-patterns resulted from N- and C-terminal antibodies colocalized very well (Figure 1I).
evidence: Colocalization observed in dual-labeling experiments shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The C-terminal 129 amino acid fragment of Giantin (mScarlet-Giantin-C129) has a localization quotient (LQ) similar to native Giantin.
source: Second, the C-terminal 129 amino acid fragment of Giantin (mScarlet-Giantin-C129), which has a LQ similar to native Giantin (Table 1), displayed almost the same ring-pattern as the N-terminal antibody (hereafter Giantin antibody unless indicated otherwise) (Figure 1J).
evidence: LQ values from Table 1 and imaging data from Figure 1J.

claim: The N- and C-termini of GM130 show overlapping ring-patterns.
source: Third, similarly, the N- and C-termini of other Golgins such as GM130 and GCC185 also showed overlapping ring-patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The N- and C-termini of GCC185 show overlapping ring-patterns.

claim: Ensemble-averaged Golgins, as visualized in bulk by light microscopy, appear to have closely adjacent N- and C-termini.

claim: The ring-pattern staining of Giantin closely represents the cisternal rim.
source: Therefore, the ring-pattern staining of Giantin should closely represent the cisternal rim.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence about Giantin N- and C-terminal colocalization.

claim: MGAT2 localizes to the interior of Giantin-rings.

claim: There are at least two types of lateral localizations in the Golgi: rim and interior.

evidence: Conclusion drawn from the contrasting localization patterns of Giantin and MGAT2.

evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F.

claim: MGAT4B appears as an inner-ring concentric to the corresponding Giantin-ring.
source: In contrast to trafficking components, our Golgi enzymes and SLC35C1 localized within Giantin-rings as a central disk in en face views (Figure 1K; Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–T), except Man1B1, ManII, MGAT4B and TPST2, which mostly appear as an inner-ring concentric to the corresponding Giantin-ring (Figure 4E,F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F.

claim: TPST2 appears as an inner-ring concentric to the corresponding Giantin-ring.
source: In contrast to trafficking components, our Golgi enzymes and SLC35C1 localized within Giantin-rings as a central disk in en face views (Figure 1K; Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–T), except Man1B1, ManII, MGAT4B and TPST2, which mostly appear as an inner-ring concentric to the corresponding Giantin-ring (Figure 4E,F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F.

claim: MGAT2-Myc and MGAT4B-AcGFP1 have almost the same LQs as Giantin (mean values: 0.53 and 0.50 vs 0.57 respectively).
source: Since MGAT2-Myc and MGAT4B-AcGFP1 had almost the same LQs as Giantin (mean values: 0.53 and 0.50 vs 0.57 respectively) (Table 1), a significant amount of these proteins are expected to reside in the same cisternae.
evidence: LQ measurements from Table 1.

claim: MGAT2 and MGAT4B mainly localize to the interior of cisternae as a central disk and inner-ring, respectively, within the Giantin-rim in the same cisternae.
source: The lateral distribution pattern of MGAT2 and MGAT4B suggests that they should mainly localize to the interior of cisternae as a central disk and inner-ring, respectively, within the Giantin-rim in the same cisternae (Figure 4G).
evidence: Inference from imaging data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: β4GalT3 and ST6Gal1 localize to shared and distinct domains within Giantin-rings.
source: Enzymes, such as β4GalT3 and ST6Gal1, which have similar LQs (Table 1), were observed to localize to shared and distinct domains within Giantin-rings (Figure 4H).
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 4H combined with LQ data from Table 1.

claim: 93% of Golgi stacks (n = 58) showed an enrichment of MGAT2 in the cisternal interior by EM.
source: To substantiate our light microscopic data, we examined the localization of MGAT2-APEX2-GFP in the native Golgi by EM. 93% (n = 58) of Golgi stacks showed an enrichment of MGAT2 in the cisternal interior (Figure 4I; Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C), which is in contrast to the staining pattern observed for GPP130 (Figure 1G).
evidence: EM data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: APEX2-generated electron density was found in vesicles and budding profiles at the rim in MGAT2-APEX2-GFP expressing cells.
source: Noticeably, APEX2-generated electron density was also found in vesicles and budding profiles at the rim (arrow heads in Figure 4I).
evidence: EM data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Golgi enzymes might be depleted from the rim either by retrieval to the interior or by sorting into membrane carriers.
source: Although the identity and destiny of these vesicles are currently unknown, our observations suggest that Golgi enzymes might be depleted from the rim either by retrieval to the interior or by sorting into membrane carriers.
evidence: Speculation based on observed EM patterns of MGAT2 localization.

claim: Golgi enzymes mainly localize to the interior of medial and trans-cisternae as a concentric disk or inner-ring.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that Golgi enzymes mainly localize to the interior of medial and trans-cisternae as a concentric disk or inner-ring, while trafficking machinery components exhibit rim localization.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple imaging experiments.

claim: Trafficking machinery components exhibit rim localization.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that Golgi enzymes mainly localize to the interior of medial and trans-cisternae as a concentric disk or inner-ring, while trafficking machinery components exhibit rim localization.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple imaging experiments.

claim: Cis-cisternae have smaller diameters than medial ones.
source: Interestingly, it also reveals that cis-cisternae have smaller diameters than medial ones, consistent with many EM thin-section or tomographic 3D images (Bykov et al., 2017; Engel et al., 2015; Staehelin and Kang, 2008), though the biological significance of which remains to be further investigated.
evidence: Observation from Figure 4J supported by references to Bykov et al., 2017, Engel et al., 2015, and Staehelin and Kang, 2008.

claim: In the less dense region of the native Golgi, Giantin and GPP130 staining appear as distinctive ring- or loop-patterns.
source: In the less dense region, Giantin and GPP130 staining appeared as distinctive ring- or loop-patterns, with β4GalT3 and GM130 filling the interior (Figure 4K,L), similar to the nocodazole-induced mini-stack.
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 4K,L.

claim: β4GalT3 and GM130 fill the interior of Giantin and GPP130 rings in the native Golgi.
source: In the less dense region, Giantin and GPP130 staining appeared as distinctive ring- or loop-patterns, with β4GalT3 and GM130 filling the interior (Figure 4K,L), similar to the nocodazole-induced mini-stack.
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 4K,L.

claim: Giantin and GPP130 positive curvy lines correspond to the rim of cisternae in oblique or en face views, not side views or cross-sections.
source: In most cases, Giantin and GPP130 positive curvy lines did not correspond to side views or cross-sections of Golgi stacks. Instead, they corresponded to the rim of cisternae in oblique or en face views (arrows in Figure 4L).
evidence: Imaging data and interpretation shown in Figure 4L.

claim: CD59 was first detected in the interior of cis-Golgi cisternae after 10 min of chase in the RUSH system.
source: The RUSH reporter CD59, a GPI-anchored protein, was first detected in the interior of cis-Golgi cisternae after 10 min of chase (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: RUSH assay data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: CD59 remained in the interior during its transition through the Golgi mini-stack.
source: During its transition through the Golgi mini-stack, as evidenced in its LQ versus time plot (Figure 5B), CD59 remained in the interior (Figure 5A), although its total intensity in Golgi mini-stacks initially increased and subsequently decreased due to the export toward the PM.
evidence: RUSH assay data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: At the later stage of the chase, there were CD59 positive puncta and tubular profiles outside Giantin-rings, which were likely Golgi-derived exocytic transport carriers.
source: At the later stage of the chase, there were CD59 positive puncta and tubular profiles outside Giantin-rings, which were likely Golgi-derived exocytic transport carriers (Figure 5A, arrows in 60 min).
evidence: RUSH assay data shown in Figure 5A with interpretation.

claim: mCherry-GPI started to appear in the interior of the Golgin84-ring 6 min after chase in live-cell super-resolution imaging.
source: Similarly, in live-cell super-resolution imaging, RUSH reporter mCherry-GPI started to appear in the interior of the Golgin84-ring 6 min after chase; it remained there for >30 min before disappearing due to post-Golgi exocytic trafficking (Figure 5C; Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—video 1.

claim: mCherry-GPI remained in the interior of the Golgin84-ring for >30 min before disappearing due to post-Golgi exocytic trafficking.
source: Similarly, in live-cell super-resolution imaging, RUSH reporter mCherry-GPI started to appear in the interior of the Golgin84-ring 6 min after chase; it remained there for >30 min before disappearing due to post-Golgi exocytic trafficking (Figure 5C; Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—video 1.

claim: Transmembrane RUSH reporters E-cadherin, VSVG, and CD8a-Furin follow similar lateral localization patterns during their intra-Golgi trafficking.
source: Transmembrane RUSH reporters, E-cadherin, VSVG and CD8a-Furin, and a soluble secretory reporter, signal peptide fused GFP, followed similar lateral localization pattern during their intra-Golgi trafficking (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: RUSH assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: A soluble secretory reporter, signal peptide fused GFP, follows similar lateral localization patterns during its intra-Golgi trafficking.
source: Transmembrane RUSH reporters, E-cadherin, VSVG and CD8a-Furin, and a soluble secretory reporter, signal peptide fused GFP, followed similar lateral localization pattern during their intra-Golgi trafficking (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: RUSH assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Conventional secretory cargos partition to the interior of the cisternae during their Golgi transition.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrated that conventional secretory cargos partition to the interior of the cisternae during their Golgi transition.
evidence: Summary conclusion from RUSH assay experiments.

claim: The secretory cargo wave does not grossly affect the interior distribution of Golgi enzymes, as evidenced by ST6Gal1.
source: The secretory cargo wave does not seem to grossly affect the interior distribution of Golgi enzymes, as evidenced by ST6Gal1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: >85% of ST6Gal1-moxGFP remained in the interior during the Golgi transition of synchronized VSVG.
source: By image quantification, >85% of ST6Gal1-moxGFP was found to remain in the interior during the Golgi transition of synchronized VSVG, although a small fluctuation (<4%) was noticed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: A previous EM study observed the shift of Golgi enzymes from the rim to the interior under a traffic wave.
source: Our finding is different from a previous EM study, in which the shift of Golgi enzymes from the rim to the interior was observed under a traffic wave (Kweon et al., 2004).
evidence: Reference to published work by Kweon et al., 2004.

claim: Rothman lab previously proposed that large secretory protein aggregates are segregated to the cisternal rim based on EM data.
source: Based on EM data, Rothman lab previously proposed that large secretory protein aggregates are segregated to the cisternal rim (Lavieu et al., 2013).
evidence: Reference to published work by Lavieu et al., 2013.

claim: Golgi-transiting GFP-collagenX appeared either diffuse or punctate.
source: We observed that Golgi-transiting GFP-collagenX appeared either diffuse or punctate (Figure 5D).
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Golgi-transiting GFP-collagenX puncta had 190 ± 20 copies (n = 77).
source: Assuming that Golgi-localized GFP-collagenX puncta were single multimeric aggregates, using GFP-tagged nucleoporin Nup133 as an in vivo GFP fluorescence standard, we estimated that Golgi-transiting GFP-collagenX puncta had 190 ± 20 copies (n = 77) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Throughout its intra-Golgi trafficking, collagenX was excluded from the interior of Giantin-rings.
source: Throughout its intra-Golgi trafficking, collagenX, either in punctate or diffuse appearance, was excluded from the interior of Giantin-rings, where co-expressed mCherry-GPI clearly localized (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: RUSH assay data shown in Figure 5D–F.

claim: CollagenX always resided at the rim, either colocalizing with Giantin or surrounding Giantin-rings as discrete puncta.
source: Instead, it always resided at the rim, either colocalizing with Giantin or surrounding Giantin-rings as discrete puncta.
evidence: Observation from RUSH assay experiments.

claim: Re-aggregated GFP-FM4-CD8a Golgi puncta upon D/D washout were estimated to have 830 ± 30 (n = 184) copies.
source: Using this protocol, the re-aggregated GFP-FM4-CD8a and FM4-moxGFP Golgi puncta upon D/D washout were estimated to have 830 ± 30 (n = 184) and 660 ± 50 (n = 127) copies, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: Re-aggregated FM4-moxGFP Golgi puncta upon D/D washout were estimated to have 660 ± 50 (n = 127) copies.
source: Using this protocol, the re-aggregated GFP-FM4-CD8a and FM4-moxGFP Golgi puncta upon D/D washout were estimated to have 830 ± 30 (n = 184) and 660 ± 50 (n = 127) copies, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: When in the de-aggregated state, both soluble and membrane FM4-chimeras localize to the interior of Giantin-rings.
source: We observed that, when in the de-aggregated state, both soluble and membrane FM4-chimeras localized to the interior of Giantin-rings (Figure 5G; Figure 5—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Once aggregated, FM4-chimeras partition to the rim as discrete puncta.
source: Intriguingly, once aggregated, they partitioned to the rim as discrete puncta.
evidence: Observation from aggregation experiments.

claim: Large cargos preferentially partition to the cisternal rim, possibly due to their bulky sizes.
source: Therefore, our light microscopic data indicated that large cargos preferentially partition to the cisternal rim, possibly due to their bulky sizes, while conventional or small cargos tend to locate to the interior.
evidence: Conclusion from cargo localization experiments with speculation about mechanism.

claim: Conventional or small cargos tend to locate to the interior of cisternae.
source: Therefore, our light microscopic data indicated that large cargos preferentially partition to the cisternal rim, possibly due to their bulky sizes, while conventional or small cargos tend to locate to the interior.
evidence: Conclusion from cargo localization experiments.

claim: Rim partitioning of large secretory cargos has previously been noted by EM.
source: Rim partitioning of large secretory cargos has previously been noted by EM (Bonfanti et al., 1998; Engel et al., 2015; Lavieu et al., 2013; Volchuk et al., 2000).
evidence: References to Bonfanti et al., 1998, Engel et al., 2015, Lavieu et al., 2013, and Volchuk et al., 2000.

claim: The study directly visualizes by light microscopy the size-dependent lateral partitioning of secretory cargos within the Golgi stack.
source: Here, we directly visualized by light microscopy the size-dependent lateral partitioning of secretory cargos within the Golgi stack.
evidence: Summary of the study's contribution.

claim: The findings provide important insight into the structure and organization of the Golgi complex.
source: Nonetheless, our findings provide important insight into the structure and organization of the Golgi complex.
evidence: Summary statement about the study's significance.

claim: Cisternal rims are dilated with a width of ~100 nm.
source: EM studies have revealed that cisternal rims are dilated with a width of ~100 nm, while their stacked interiors are narrow and tightly spaced with a width of ~20 nm (Bykov et al., 2017; Engel et al., 2015; Staehelin and Kang, 2008).
evidence: References to Bykov et al., 2017, Engel et al., 2015, and Staehelin and Kang, 2008.

claim: Stacked cisternal interiors are narrow and tightly spaced with a width of ~20 nm.
source: EM studies have revealed that cisternal rims are dilated with a width of ~100 nm, while their stacked interiors are narrow and tightly spaced with a width of ~20 nm (Bykov et al., 2017; Engel et al., 2015; Staehelin and Kang, 2008).
evidence: References to Bykov et al., 2017, Engel et al., 2015, and Staehelin and Kang, 2008.

claim: Zipper-like intracisternal and intercisternal protein arrays have been discovered at interior regions of medial and trans-cisternae in green alga through cryo-electron tomography.
source: Recently, zipper-like intracisternal and intercisternal protein arrays have been discovered at interior regions of medial and trans-cisternae in green alga through the cryo-electron tomography (Engel et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to published work by Engel et al., 2015.

claim: It was proposed that tightly packed protein arrays comprise Golgi enzymes.
source: It was proposed that these tightly packed protein arrays comprise Golgi enzymes.
evidence: Reference to a hypothesis from the literature.

claim: Super-resolution and EM data from the Golgi mini-stack provide direct evidence supporting the hypothesis that protein arrays comprise Golgi enzymes.
source: Our super-resolution and EM data from the Golgi mini-stack provide direct evidence supporting this hypothesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's data.

claim: Enzyme-arrays might organize as an 'enzyme matrix' to stack cisternal membrane, retain Golgi enzymes or accessory proteins, and exclude trafficking machinery components by a possible molecular crowding mechanism.
source: These enzyme-arrays might organize as an 'enzyme matrix' to 1) stack cisternal membrane, 2) retain Golgi enzymes or accessory proteins and 3) exclude trafficking machinery components by a possible molecular crowding mechanism.
evidence: Speculation about the function of enzyme arrays.

claim: Collectively, Golgi enzymes determine and maintain the characteristic structure of the Golgi complex.
source: Therefore, it seems that, collectively, Golgi enzymes determine and maintain the characteristic structure of the Golgi complex.
evidence: Inference from the proposed role of enzyme matrices.

claim: Most secretory cargos in higher eukaryotes undergo glycosylation in the Golgi complex.
source: Most secretory cargos in higher eukaryotes undergo glycosylation in the Golgi complex.
evidence: General knowledge about secretory cargo processing.

claim: Secretory cargos must access interior domains of different cisternae and reside there long enough for sequential glycosylation.
source: Our finding that the cisternal interior and rim correspond to processing and transport domain, respectively, implies that secretory cargos must access interior domains of different cisternae and then reside there long enough for sequential glycosylation.
evidence: Logical inference from the spatial organization findings.

claim: Conventional cargos have a sufficiently short residence time in the cisternal rim, where they are either retrieved and retained by the 'enzyme matrix' to the interior or packed into membrane carriers targeting to the PM at the trans-Golgi.
source: On the other hand, these cargos probably have a sufficiently short residence time in the cisternal rim, in which they are either retrieved and retained by the 'enzyme matrix' to the interior or packed into membrane carriers targeting to the PM at the trans-Golgi.
evidence: Inference from cargo localization patterns.

claim: The retention by the 'enzyme matrix' occurs by default and is independent of glycosylation.
source: It seems that the retention by the 'enzyme matrix' occurs by default and is independent of glycosylation because secretory GFP is preferentially found within the cisternal interior.
evidence: Inference from the observation that secretory GFP localizes to the interior.

claim: Bulky cargos might be incompatible with the crowded molecular environment of the tightly packed 'enzyme matrix' and/or the narrow luminal space at the interior.
source: These observations suggest that bulky cargos might be incompatible with the crowded molecular environment of the tightly packed 'enzyme matrix' and/or the narrow luminal space at the interior, which can have a width of <10 nm (Engel et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculation based on cargo localization patterns and reference to Engel et al., 2015.

claim: The study directly demonstrates the spatial separation of processing and transport functions within the Golgi complex.
source: Our study therefore directly demonstrates the spatial separation of processing and transport functions within the Golgi complex.
evidence: Summary statement of the main finding from the abstract.

claim: The nocodazole-induced Golgi mini-stack is a valid model of the native Golgi.
source: There have been extensive evidences demonstrating that the nocodazole-induced Golgi mini-stack is a valid model of the native Golgi (Cole et al., 1996; Rogalski et al., 1984; Trucco et al., 2004; Van De Moortele et al., 1993) and we have previously discussed its advantages in studying the molecular and spatial organization of the Golgi (Tie et al., 2017; Tie et al., 2016b).
evidence: References to Cole et al., 1996, Rogalski et al., 1984, Trucco et al., 2004, Van De Moortele et al., 1993, Tie et al., 2017, and Tie et al., 2016b.

claim: The Golgi complex is one of the most important processing and sorting stations along the secretory and endocytic pathway.
source: The Golgi complex is one of the most important processing and sorting stations along the secretory and endocytic pathway (Glick and Luini, 2011; Klumperman, 2011; Lu and Hong, 2014).
evidence: References to Glick and Luini, 2011, Klumperman, 2011, and Lu and Hong, 2014.

claim: In mammalian cells, the Golgi complex consists of a network of laterally linked Golgi stacks.
source: In mammalian cells, it consists of a network of laterally linked Golgi stacks.
evidence: General knowledge about Golgi structure.

claim: A Golgi stack comprises 4–7 flattened cisternae and can be divided into cis, medial and trans-regions.
source: As the structural unit, a Golgi stack comprises 4–7 flattened cisternae and can be divided into cis, medial and trans-regions.
evidence: General knowledge about Golgi structure.

claim: The trans-Golgi region further develops into the trans-Golgi network (TGN).
source: The trans-Golgi region further develops into the trans-Golgi network (TGN).
evidence: General knowledge about Golgi structure.

claim: The cis-Golgi receives secretory cargos from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) exit site (ERES) and ER Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC).
source: It is known that the cis-Golgi receives secretory cargos from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) exit site (ERES) and ER Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC), while the trans-Golgi and TGN exchange materials with endosomes and the plasma membrane (PM).
evidence: General knowledge about Golgi function.

claim: The trans-Golgi and TGN exchange materials with endosomes and the plasma membrane (PM).
source: It is known that the cis-Golgi receives secretory cargos from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) exit site (ERES) and ER Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC), while the trans-Golgi and TGN exchange materials with endosomes and the plasma membrane (PM).
evidence: General knowledge about Golgi function.

claim: It has been hypothesized that the two principal functions of the Golgi, processing and transport, are spatially organized for optimal efficiency.
source: It has been hypothesized that the two principal functions of the Golgi, processing and transport, are spatially organized for optimal efficiency (Patterson et al., 2008).
evidence: Reference to published work by Patterson et al., 2008.

claim: Such molecular organization across the Golgi stack has not been directly demonstrated prior to this study.
source: However, such molecular organization across the Golgi stack has not been directly demonstrated.
evidence: Statement about the gap in knowledge that this study addresses.
